claims.text: Differences in the reduction potentials and reduction rates of metal precursors can cause phase separation during high-entropy alloy nanoparticle synthesis.
Low-temperature solution reduction synchronizes the reduction kinetics of different noble-metal precursors.
Synchronized precursor reduction overcomes intrinsic differences in reduction potentials.
Coordinated nucleation and growth produce homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
High-temperature processing tends to cause rapid, asynchronous reduction that favors elemental segregation and phase separation.
High-entropy alloy nanoparticles can be synthesized using solution-based low-temperature methods.
Temperatures up to approximately 200 degrees Celsius constitute the proposed mild solution-reduction regime.
Synchronized reduction prevents premature or differential precursor conversion and thereby produces uniform nucleation.
Lower thermal energy moderates and equalizes the reduction rates of different metal ions.
Early reduction of one metal species seeds phase-separated growth.
Concurrent nucleation across metal species yields a well-mixed, single-phase alloy.
Low-temperature solution synthesis will yield more uniform elemental distributions and less phase separation than high-temperature flash synthesis.
Low-temperature solution synthesis permits controlled nanoparticle dimensions.
Carbothermal shock and microwave heating are established baselines that exhibit elemental segregation and phase inhomogeneity.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal nanoparticle systems made from soluble precursors whose reduction behavior can be moderated.
The mechanism may fail when constituent elements have irreconcilably different reduction kinetics.
The mechanism may not apply to non-solvated or refractory precursors.
The factors governing phase formation during low-temperature high-entropy alloy nanoparticle synthesis remain unclear.
